title: From Satisfaction to Portfolio Strategy
text:
Why this research?
The Partnerships & Rewards Strategy team needs evidence for two jobs.
Evaluate the current portfolio. How satisfied are members? Where is friction occurring? Which problems are fixable?
Shape the future portfolio. Which reward models should be continued and scaled? Which successful mechanics might be replicated elsewhere? Which rewards should be fundamentally redesigned—or dropped?



SCALE & REPLICATE
Learn what makes the strongest experiences work and use those characteristics to inspire adjacent partnerships.



FIX
Protect propositions that create value, but remove targeting, eligibility or journey friction.



RETHINK
Identify rewards where the basic experience is failing and decide whether to remediate, redesign or discontinue.




CSAT is one input, not the entire commercial decision. A real portfolio review would also consider redemption, economics, reach, strategic fit and operational feasibility.

title: From Satisfaction to Portfolio Strategy
section: StreamPlus: the average hides two completely different experiences
text:
StreamPlus: the average hides two completely different experiences
The clearest way to tell the StreamPlus story is not with theme counts. It is to show how sharply the experience changes depending on whether a member can actually benefit from the offer.


Code
stream_segment_plot <- stream |>
  mutate(
    subscriber_group = if_else(existing_streamplus_subscriber == "Yes", "Existing subscriber", "Not already subscribed"),
    experience = case_when(csat_score <= 2 ~ "Dissatisfied (1–2)", csat_score == 3 ~ "Neutral (3)", TRUE ~ "Satisfied (4–5)"),
    experience = factor(experience, levels = c("Dissatisfied (1–2)", "Neutral (3)", "Satisfied (4–5)"))
  ) |>
  count(subscriber_group, experience) |>
  group_by(subscriber_group) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(stream_segment_plot, aes(x = pct, y = fct_rev(factor(subscriber_group)), fill = experience)) +
  geom_col(width = .62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = if_else(pct >= .08, percent(pct, accuracy = 1), "")), position = position_stack(vjust = .5), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Dissatisfied (1–2)" = "#B74D3E", "Neutral (3)" = "#B9B2A3", "Satisfied (4–5)" = "#557A46")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL, title = "StreamPlus is a targeting problem, not a weak proposition", subtitle = "Existing subscribers are far more likely to be dissatisfied; members who are not already subscribed respond very positively.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16))















NoteWhat the segmentation changes



For members who are not already subscribed, StreamPlus behaves like a strong reward. For existing subscribers, the same offer often has little incremental value.
That changes the management response from “improve the reward” to “improve who receives it.” APacks should work with CRM and Data Analytics to identify likely eligibility before the offer is surfaced, while Partnerships should negotiate a viable alternative benefit for existing subscribers.

title: From Satisfaction to Portfolio Strategy
text:
The bigger strategic opportunity






TipTurn one CSAT study into a reward-design playbook



Taken together, the five rewards begin to define what APacks should look for when designing, evaluating or negotiating partner rewards.
Make the value obvious. DineLocal shows the strength of an easy-to-understand reward with flexible, relevant value.
Match the reward to the member. StreamPlus shows that a strong proposition can become a poor experience when eligibility is ignored.
Design for the market, not just the global proposition. MoveNow shows how local coverage can materially change the same reward.
Treat the journey as part of the reward. FitLife shows that activation, access and renewal mechanics can suppress an otherwise useful proposition.
Protect the basics. FoodDrop shows that no amount of strategic fit compensates for unreliable redemption or unexpected restrictions.

title: From Satisfaction to Portfolio Strategy
text:
From measurement to organisational capability
The longer-term opportunity is to turn these principles into a shared evidence base for reward strategy.
That gives Partnerships clearer criteria when evaluating and negotiating new offers. It gives Markets and Membership Leads a framework for judging whether a reward will work locally. It gives CRM and Data Analytics a clearer role in matching rewards to eligible and relevant audiences. It gives Membership Experience and Operations concrete experience standards to protect. And it gives senior strategic leaders a more consistent way to compare partnership opportunities beyond commercial terms alone.
In that sense, the value of the research is not simply deciding what to do with today’s five partners. It is beginning to define the characteristics APacks should seek—and the questions it should ask—whenever it considers the next reward.

title: From Satisfaction to Portfolio Strategy
text:
The bigger strategic opportunity






TipTurn one CSAT study into a reward-design playbook



This study does more than identify a winner and two problem rewards. It gives APacks the starting point for defining what a strong partner reward looks like.
Is the value obvious? Members should immediately understand what they receive and why it is worthwhile.
Is it broadly usable—or precisely targeted? A reward can be excellent and still fail if it is shown to members who cannot benefit from it.
Is redemption genuinely low-friction? Promised value only matters if members can successfully realise it.
Does it fit the member and the market? Coverage, availability and local relevance can determine whether the same proposition succeeds across markets.
Can APacks learn from the mechanic, not just the partner? Strong rewards can become templates for exploring adjacent categories rather than isolated successes.
